title: Free to choose (5:1)
hookLine: every person is given free will; this is a great principle
tomorrow: if God knows what i'll choose, am i still choosing?

cards: It's how I'm wired. My family's just like this. That's my sign, so of course I'm stubborn.
Reasons like these are easy to reach for when a choice gets hard. Some of them hold a little truth. But is the choice to change really yours?
Maimonides opens chapter five by answering that before anything else, and he doesn't hedge.

teach.h: THE POWER IS IN YOUR HAND.
teach.b: Freedom, he writes, is given to every person. If someone wants to turn toward the good and be righteous, the power is in their hand. If they want to turn the other way, that's in their hand too.

He reads a strange verse from the garden this way: "Behold, the man is become as one of us, to know good and evil." Humans, he says, know good and evil from within themselves, and nobody holds their hand back.
Then he names the idea he's arguing against.
Don't believe, he says, that God decrees at a person's birth whether they'll be righteous or wicked.
Every person can become righteous like Moses or wicked like Jeroboam, wise or foolish, merciful or cruel.
And he calls this a great principle, a pillar of the whole Torah, because commands only make sense if you can choose to keep them.
His verse is from Deuteronomy: "See, I have set before thee this day life and good, and death and evil." Set before thee. Not decided for you.
That's why return, all those chapters of it, is possible at all. Wiring and family and habits are real pressures. But in Maimonides' picture, they push.

how: Free will is a foundation of Jewish teaching on return; the Torah portion with 'I have set before thee life and good' (Nitzavim) is read in synagogue shortly before Rosh Hashanah.

o: every person's path is fixed before they are born
every person can do as they wish without judgment
every person can turn toward good or away from it

s: in Judaism, whether you'll be good or bad is decided before you're born
Maimonides calls that idea one not to believe: anyone can become righteous like Moses or wicked like Jeroboam.
Maimonides calls free choice a pillar of the Torah
he calls it a great principle, a pillar of the Torah and its commands.
free choice means family and habits have no pull at all
the lesson's point: pressures are real, but in Maimonides' picture they don't decide.

games.q: your friend says her short temper is 'just how she was born, nothing to do about it.' which reply fits Maimonides?
o: anyone can become merciful or cruel; the turning is in her hands.
she's right; temper is fixed at birth, so she can only manage around it.
only God can change it; trying on her own won't make a difference.
games.why: Maimonides: no one is decreed righteous or wicked at birth; every person can become wise or foolish, merciful or cruel.

practice: Take a pen. Write one small choice waiting for you today, then write the words I choose, and finish the sentence on purpose rather than by default.
Read it back once, slowly, and sit with the feel of a decision that's actually yours.

wordCard.voice: Free to choose: Maimonides' great principle. Freedom is given to every person to turn toward good or away from it, and nothing is decreed at birth.

orig.note: Hebrew: freedom, permission; Maimonides writes that it is given to every person.

carryVoice: Your line: free to choose. Wiring and habits push hard, but they don't decide. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilkhot Teshuvah 5:1–3 (freedom given to every person; nothing decreed at birth; a great principle, a pillar of Torah)
